newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa's Mbeki launches "Cycles for Africa".
newsitem.headline: South Africa's Mbeki launches "Cycles for Africa".

text.p: Bicycles from Japan rode in circles around a school made of old ocean containers on Thursday in a modest but potent form of black empowerment for this sprawling shantytown north of Johannesburg.

South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, who was too poor to have a bike in his school days, inaugurated the "Cycle Aid for Africa" programme in Ivory Park, turning over two-wheelers discarded by the city of Osaka to delighted primary pupils.
In a country where thousands must walk stoically for miles and miles to reach a job, a shop or a school, the humble bicycle is prized as the cheapest possible means of transport.

"The system of apartheid ensured that not enough schools were provided for the majority of the population who had to spend hours walking to and from school rather than in the classroom itself," said Mbeki, heir apparent to President Nelson Mandela when the president steps down in two years.
"This project is a practical way in which we seek to empower communities in their quest for better education."

Among the packing-crate and plastic-bag huts of South Africa's "informal settlements", as squatter camps are called, working bicycles are a rare sight. The refurbished Japanese models, some still bearing their Osaka licence stickers, brought admiring glances from parents as well as schoolchildren.
"I'm told there's another 100,000 discarded bicycles lying in a warehouse in Osaka," said Mbeki, joined by Japanese ambassador Yoshizo Konishi for the launch of the project at the Rebonwe school.

"This is a great idea and I hope we'll all get one. Look here, it has a basket to carry coke and cakes," said Jackie Metsa, a 12-year-old school prefect. A classmate, Sbusiso Mngomezulu, added conscientiously that "it will be great for going to the shops for my mother".
The project is backed by Education Africa, a non-governmental organisation, and sponsored by South African Airways and Safmarine, the merchant shipping line, which brought the bikes from Japan.
Safmarine also supplied the slightly battered oceangoing containers which, welded together and illuminated by cut-out windows, form Rebonwe school.
Its neat, blue-painted cluster of boxy steel rooms looked far too small for the 800 registered pupils, but the muddy schoolyard was too big for Mbeki, whose dark secret came out.
Talented as he may be in politics, government and public speaking, it appears that Mandela's preferred candidate for the presidency of South Africa cannot ride a bike.
"Now for the difficult part of my visit today," he said at the end of a short speech. "Do you really want to see?"
A chorus of shrill voices left him no way out. Manfully, Mbeki went for a "test ride" -- but never got both feet off the ground.
